Hi Daniel,

Thanks again for the time today. As promised, attaching a quick note on how we handle usage that goes above reserved commits for Dedicated GPU pools at Redwood. High level: customers can provision a committed GPU pool (monthly/annual) with predictable throughput. We offer three mechanisms for handling activity above that commit:

- Grace buffer (short automatic burst credit to absorb traffic spikes)
- Metered excess billing (per GPU-hour / per token equivalent)
- Soft throttling (progressive rate limiting after buffer depletion to preserve SLOs for committed tenants)

Can you confirm the team’s main concern is whether spikes will be billed immediately versus throttled? If you can share a 30-day tail of peak throughput (or permit us to inspect the trial logs), Marcus can size a recommended commit that minimizes excess.

I’ve attached a draft SLA and a pricing tiers sheet for reference. If you’d like, we can lock the overage rate for the first 6 months as part of an introductory concession while you ramp.

Next steps: let me know a time for a 30-minute follow-up with Marcus and Neha this week.

Hi Daniel — quick technical summary from the runtime/serving side. TL;DR: we separate billing from protective throttling and provide predictable burst behavior. Details: 

1) Buffer & burst model
- Each committed pool gets a rolling burst buffer (expressed in GPU-minutes) sized by commit level and historical tail behavior. The buffer is intended for short spikes (seconds->hours).
- Buffer consumption is FIFO across routes; it refills slowly (on the order of a few hours under normal traffic).

2) Metering granularity
- We meter per-GPU-minute and per-token equivalence for generation workloads. Excess billing is calculated hourly but reported with minute granularity in the console so you can reconcile usage.

3) Throttling policy
- Soft throttle: after buffer exhaustion, we enter a tiered soft-throttle for new request admission. In-flight requests continue to completion at the current allocated rate (we do not drop in-flight tokens mid-response).
- Hard throttle: protection-level hard throttles are only engaged when the pool reaches safety limits for hardware (rare) — these are communicated via 429 and backoff headers with expected retry windows.

4) Pricing implications for prolonged overage (e.g., 20–40% monthly)
- For predictable, repeatable overages, we recommend re-sizing the commit (saves 20–40% vs metered excess).
- If re-sizing is not possible, we offer a stepped metered rate: list excess rate for ad-hoc spikes; a negotiated tiered rate for repeatable monthly windows (this is a commercial option Neha can enable).

5) Impact on latency and SLOs
- The buffer and soft-throttle are designed to preserve tail latency for committed tenants. Soft throttles preferentially limit the admission of new heavy requests (long-context, high-batch) while preserving in-flight shorter requests.

If you share the 30-day peak export, I’ll run a quick simulation and provide a recommended commit + expected monthly excess under current traffic.

Marcus
Senior Engineer, Serving Runtime

Hi Daniel — commercial here. Based on Marcus’s timeline, two paths we commonly offer:

A) Commit + reserved burst credits (recommended for predictable monthly overage)
- 12-month commit: baseline discount 18% off public list, includes a monthly burst buffer and capped excess rate at 1.25x list for the first 6 months.
- 24-month commit: baseline discount 25%, larger buffer, capped excess at 1.15x list for 12 months.

B) Flexible commit + negotiated excess rate (recommended when you can’t re-size immediately)
- Lower baseline discount (10–15%) but a negotiated per-GPU-hour excess rate tied to usage bands (0–10%, 10–30%, 30%+). Example: 0–10% billed at 0.9x list, 10–30% billed at 1.0x list, 30%+ billed at 1.2x list.

Operational items:
- We can include a 90-day ramp clause that caps the first 90 days of excess billing at 1.1x list while you stabilize.
- All excess is visible in the console with minute granularity and a downloadable CSV for finance reconciliation.

If you’re comfortable, we can draft an amendment with the 12‑month commit + 6‑month capped overage concession as a starting point. Soojin, are there legal constraints on the capped-excess language?

-Neha
Director, Revenue Operations
